headline_en: Heart health will improve with pomegranates and walnuts
summary_en: Scientists at King's College London have made an important discovery regarding heart disease. They found that after eating pomegranates, walnuts, and certain berries, a natural substance called Urolithin A is formed in our bodies. This substance can improve the heart's function by up to eighty percent. This discovery could be especially helpful for a type of heart failure for which treatment options are currently very limited. According to scientists, this natural compound can bring a major improvement to heart health. This substance formed in the body from pomegranates and walnuts could pave a new way for the treatment of heart failure in the future.

headline_hi: अस्पताल में मशीनों का शोर हुआ शांत
headline_en: Machine noise silenced in the hospital
summary_en: The UK's Royal Cornwall Hospitals NHS Trust has launched a new initiative to reduce noise in hospitals. They started the 'Silent Hospital Pilot Project' in the year 2023. This three-year study focuses on reducing alarm sounds and noise pollution in wards. Here, instead of suppressing sound, it is sent to the right place like data. In hospital ICUs, there is constant noise of fifty to seventy decibels, and at times it reaches eighty to one hundred decibels. Meanwhile, according to the World Health Organization, a sound level of thirty decibels is considered ideal for rest. Hospital staff have to listen to hundreds of alarms during every shift, up to ninety percent of which do not require any medical attention. The results of this project's second phase have been so good that other UK hospitals are also preparing to adopt it.

lead.title: The Hospital That Silenced the Machines
lead.summary: B eep. Beep. Beep. The heartbeat monitor chirps. Hospitals have long tried to fight acoustic chaos with passive tactics — hanging sound-absorbing ceiling tiles, laying soft rubber flooring or begging clinical staff to whisper in the corridors. Beep. Beep. Beep. Blood pressure drops. But the Royal Cornwall Hospitals NHS Trust in the United Kingdom has been trying something different. Instead of regarding noise as an inevitable physical nuisance that needs to be muffled, it treats sound as data that can be routed. In 2023, the trust launched the Silent Hospital Pilot Project , a three-year study exploring how to target “alarm fatigue” and noise pollution on hospital wards. As the second phase of the pilot comes to an end, its outcomes have already been so promising that other hospital networks around the U.K. are preparing to follow suit. Beep. Beep. Beep. Oxygen levels dip. Hospital wards are notoriously loud, with continuous background noise on intensive care units , for example, often averaging 50 to 70 decibels (dB), comparable to heavy traffic, and sharp peaks frequently passing 80 to 100 dB, roughly the equivalent of a jackhammer. These levels vastly exceed the World Health Organization’s recommended threshold of 30 dB to be able to rest. BEEP. BEEP. BEEP. BEEP. BEEP. The monitor escalates to an urgent, repeating multi-tone musical sequence engineered to demand immediate human attention. Studies across international health systems reveal that clinical staff encounter hundreds of alarm signals per shift, up to 90 percent of which require no clinical intervention, for example because a patient mistakenly presses the buzzer when they move. headline_hi: सुपारी के पत्तों से बनी सुंदर प्लेटें
headline_en: Beautiful plates made from areca palm leaves
summary_en: Several useful ways of utilizing products from the areca nut tree are emerging in India. After harvesting areca nuts, plates are being made from the leaves that fall to the ground, and they are also used as fodder. In Mizoram, Karnataka, and Kerala, researchers and farmers have discovered many better uses for it. In Mizoram, women farmers are making biodegradable plates from leaves fallen on the ground. The Indian Council of Agricultural Research, or ICAR, has helped two groups in Kolasib and Mamit districts by providing machines. Here, women collect the fallen leaves, sort them, and dry them in the sun for at least a week. Then, plates are made using twenty and thirty centimeter dies. Between 2019 and 2022, these two groups together made more than 1.6 million plates. This has also provided tribal women with an additional source of income.

headline_hi: मूक-बधिरों के लिए अनोखा सांस्कृतिक केंद्र
headline_en: A unique cultural center for the Deaf
summary_en: Preparations are underway in the UK to build a special center for the Deaf community. This campaign has been named DeafCity Hub. Urban planner and social activist Amanpreet Arnold is leading this initiative. Amanpreet was Deaf herself from childhood and received a cochlear implant at the age of twenty-one. Around eighteen million people in the UK live with hearing loss, but across the entire country, there is not a single permanent cultural center made by and for the Deaf community. DeafCity Hub aims to create a building constructed based on DeafSpace principles. These are architectural guidelines specifically designed for Deaf people. This center will be developed into a national platform for Deaf art, culture, and community life.
source: The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News

lead.title: DeafCity Hub and the fight to build a space where sign language can live and thrive
lead.summary: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Sign language interpreters at rap concerts go viral for a reason. There’s something genuinely arresting about watching BSL in full flight: the expressiveness, the grammar operating in three-dimensional space, a face carrying as much meaning as the hands. People who’ve never encountered it before tend to stop scrolling. And then the clip ends, and the Deaf community goes back to navigating a world that wasn’t built with them in mind. Deaf culture has arguably never had more mainstream presence. Rose Ayling-Ellis won Strictly Come Dancing in 2021 and became one of the most recognized faces on British television; CODA took home the Best Picture Oscar in 2022; the British Sign Language Act received royal assent that same year, legally recognizing BSL as a language of England, Scotland, and Wales for the first time. And yet across the entire United Kingdom, with 18 million people living with some degree of hearing loss, there is not a single dedicated cultural center built for and by the Deaf community. Not a permanent one. Urban planner and activist Amanprit Arnold has been sitting with this for years. Now she’s doing something about it. Arnold was born deaf and received cochlear implants at 21. Her design agency, Disability Urbanism , advises city planners and developers on accessibility. But the DeafCity Hub campaign is different. headline_hi: बेघर कॉलेज छात्रों को मिला सुरक्षित आशियाना
headline_en: Homeless college students get a safe haven
summary_en: A new housing facility has been opened for homeless college students in Denver, USA. Depaul USA's Dax Program has launched this near the Capitol building. This program provides up to two years of housing for students who are homeless or at risk of homelessness. Here, students can stay safely and focus on their college studies without any worry. This Denver building dates back to the 1890s, where accommodation is arranged for fifteen students. The Dax Program started in the year 2015. The organization runs eleven housing facilities across Chicago, Los Angeles, Philadelphia, and New York, and has provided housing to 494 students so far. In Denver, this initiative has partnered with Metropolitan State University and Regis University. On this occasion, alumna Nikya Harrelle told the students that they are never alone.

lead.title: A Place to Sleep for Denver’s Homeless College Students
lead.summary: This story was originally published by Chalkbeat. Sign up for their newsletters at ckbe.at/newsletters. During her first semester at Chicago’s Malcolm X College, Nikya Harrell had had enough. It was winter, and she was cold. She was bouncing to and from family members’ houses and sometimes could only afford one meal a week. Harrell came to school overwhelmed and crying. A concerned friend suggested she see the school’s therapist, who connected her with the Dax Program, which offers students at risk of or experiencing homelessness a place to live for up to two years. Harrell came to Denver for Depaul USA’s Dax Program’s recent opening of the city’s first student residence near the Capitol building. Harrell had a message for other students who face challenges finding a place to live that she’s often repeated to herself: “You’re never alone.” Community members gather to bless the newly opened Depaul USA Dax Program housing on September 24, 2026, in Denver. Credit: Jason Gonzales / Chalkbeat Dax provides students with a safe living space that allows them to focus on getting a college degree without worrying about where they’ll sleep. The program has partnered with Metropolitan State University of Denver and Regis University, but wants to expand services to other local colleges and universities. The nonprofit provides resources to people experiencing homelessness and operates 11 Dax student housing programs in Chicago, Los Angeles, Philadelphia and New York. The program started in 2015 and has housed 494 students in those cities. The Denver Dax residence, an 1890s brick building that was originally a duplex in North Capitol Hill, is one of the national program’s larger residences and will be able to house up to 15 students. headline_hi: गांव की शांति ने बचाए सैकड़ों गिद्ध
headline_en: Village peace saved hundreds of vultures
summary_en: Chirgaon in Raigad district of Maharashtra has set a unique example of saving vultures. Since the year 2002, playing DJs at weddings has been completely banned in the village. Loudspeakers and loud firecrackers have also been completely stopped here during festivals. Rare species of vultures build nests and raise their young in the village trees. Before the noise stopped, only twenty-two vultures were left here. But in the latest count, the number of these vultures has risen to three hundred forty-seven. Nature lover Premsagar Mestri and the villagers worked together to protect the nests of these birds. They have also arranged a quiet environment and safe food for the birds. At a time when the country's vulture population is rapidly declining, this is a major success. Preparations are now underway to declare this area a vulture conservation reserve. This care from the villagers has proved that a little mindfulness can save lives.

lead.title: How Keeping DJs Out of Weddings Is Saving Vultures in This Maharashtra Village
lead.summary: When a wedding procession passes through Chirgaon in Maharashtra’s Raigad district, one familiar sound is missing: the DJ. Since 2002, the village has prohibited DJs and loudspeakers. Firecrackers are also restricted during festivals and other celebrations. The reason lies high up in the trees around the village, where vultures come to nest and raise their young. Two decades ago, Chirgaon’s residents were watching these birds disappear. At the time, only 22 vultures belonging to two species, the white-rumped and long-billed vultures, were recorded here. According to the last census in 2022, that number has grown to 347. The rise cannot be credited to the DJ ban alone. Over the years, Premsagar Mestri, founder of the Society of Eco-Endangered Species Conservation and Protection (SEESCAP), worked with local bird enthusiasts and villagers on several fronts. They protected nesting trees, reduced human disturbance around breeding sites and worked to make sure the vultures had access to food. Their efforts came at a time when vultures across India were facing a much larger crisis. India once had millions of vultures in the 1980s. Their numbers then fell dramatically. The decline was especially severe among white-rumped, long-billed and slender-billed vultures, with some species losing more than 90% of their populations. headline_en: Free music for twenty-one thousand children
summary_en: A non-profit organization in Miami-Dade County, USA, is providing music education to children. The organization named 'Young Musicians Unite' is running free music classes in one hundred thirty-one schools. Around twenty-one thousand students are benefiting from this wonderful program. Teachers believe that because of these music classes, it has become much easier for children to come to school and take an interest in studies. At the same time, they are also able to connect better with their school and community. This initiative has made the school environment even more pleasant and engaging for the students.
